title: The capital stack: who gets paid first, and why that sets the price
summary: The capital stack is the order in which every source of money is repaid, and therefore the order in which each one loses. Price, control and risk all follow from position in that queue. A developer who understands the queue can add capital without quietly handing someone else the keys.
body:
The capital stack is a queue: the money at the bottom is repaid first and loses last, the money at the top is repaid last and loses first. Every layer's price, and every layer's power to take control, follows from where it stands in that queue.

Recall

Q. What does the debt service coverage ratio measure?

A. Net operating income divided by annual debt service. It tells a lender how many times over the property's income covers the loan payments, and so how far income can fall before the payments are in danger.

Q. Why does a project usually sit in its own company rather than in the developer's name?

A. To ring-fence the project's liabilities, to give the lender one clean borrower to take security over, and to give investors one clean thing to own.

Q. What is revenue per available room, and why do hotel people watch it?

A. Occupancy multiplied by average daily rate. It combines how full the hotel is with how much each room earns, so it cannot be flattered by discounting to fill rooms.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, very few projects are funded with one bank loan and the developer's own cash. The gap between what the senior lender will lend and what the developer can put in is usually filled by other people's money, and each of those people arrives with a different claim, a different price and a different trigger for taking over. If you understand the stack, you can raise the money you need and still be the person running the project in a bad year. If you do not, you can sign four sets of documents that each look reasonable and discover, on the day value dips, that one of them lets a stranger replace you.

The queue, in plain English

Picture four buckets stacked one on top of another. At the bottom is the senior loan, secured by a mortgage on the land and building. Above it sits a mezzanine loan: a loan that ranks behind the senior loan and, in many deals, is secured not by the building but by a pledge of the shares or units in the company that owns the building. Above that sits preferred equity: money that is technically ownership, but which is promised its return and its capital back before the ordinary owners see anything. At the top is common equity, the developer and the ordinary investors, who are paid last and keep whatever is left.

When the project is sold or refinanced, cash flows down through the buckets from the bottom up. When value falls, losses eat down from the top. That one picture explains nearly everything else.

Here is the first worked example. Take a hypothetical project that cost 100 million dollars. The senior loan is 60 million, the mezzanine loan 15 million, preferred equity 10 million and common equity 15 million. Now suppose the finished building is worth only 80 million. The senior lender is owed 60 and is paid in full. The mezzanine lender is owed 15 and is paid in full, because value reaches 75. Preferred equity is owed 10 but only 5 remains, so it loses half. Common equity loses everything. A 20 percent fall in value wiped out the top layer completely. That is the arithmetic of standing at the back of the queue.

Price follows position

Because the top layers absorb losses first, they demand more. In commercial practice a senior construction loan prices lowest, mezzanine prices well above it, preferred equity targets more again, and common equity expects the most because it has no promised return at all. These relationships are market practice, not a rule or a standard, and the actual spreads move with the credit cycle.

The professional framing is to describe each layer by the slice of value it occupies, stated as a percentage of cost or value. In our example the senior loan covers the first 60 percent, mezzanine covers 60 to 75, preferred covers 75 to 85, and common covers 85 to 100. A lender reading that line knows instantly how much value can disappear before it loses a dollar.

The second worked example is about what the extra layers cost the common equity. If the senior loan costs a hypothetical 6 percent and the mezzanine costs a hypothetical 12 percent, then adding 15 million of mezzanine in place of 15 million of common equity saves the common investors 15 million of cash today but costs 1.8 million a year in interest. If the building earns only 7 percent on cost, that mezzanine dollar costs more than it earns. The common equity is now smaller and its return per dollar is higher if things go well, but its cash yield falls and its margin for error shrinks. Expensive capital only helps when the asset earns more than that capital costs.

Say that out loud now.

Control, not just money

The second thing position decides is who can take the wheel. The senior lender's remedy is to enforce its mortgage against the property, which usually means a court or a formal sale process and takes time. A mezzanine lender holding a pledge of the owner's shares can often enforce faster, by taking ownership of the company itself, which brings the building and the senior loan with it. A preferred equity investor usually has no security at all; its remedy is written into the partnership or operating agreement, typically a right to remove the developer as manager if payments are missed or milestones slip.

So the layer that looks junior on paper can be the one that moves first in a crisis. The document that decides how these parties behave towards each other is the intercreditor agreement, a contract between the senior lender and the mezzanine lender setting out who may do what, when, and with whose consent. We study it on day four.

How the best do it

Large institutional sponsors tend to share a habit that a small developer can copy directly. They size total leverage to a downside value, not to the most generous term sheet on the table. They decide in advance the value at which each layer above the senior loan would be impaired, and they will not accept a stack where an ordinary dip, rather than a disaster, hands control to someone else. And they insist that every junior layer is documented with the senior lender's knowledge and consent before closing, never introduced afterwards.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is stacking so high that a modest fall in value or a short delay hands control to a junior capital provider whose real business plan is to own the asset. Some junior lenders are perfectly happy to lend into that position. The control is simple to state: before you accept any layer, calculate the value and the delay at which it can take control, compare that to a sober downside case, and keep enough common equity at the top that the trigger sits well beyond a normal bad year.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the word equity in preferred equity and treats it as patient partnership money. In most deals it behaves like expensive debt with a control switch attached: a promised return, a fixed date to be repaid, and a right to remove you. Read the remedies, not the label.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: interest on loans and returns on preferred equity can be treated very differently for tax purposes, so the label on a layer can change after-tax cost; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: junior lenders often ask for personal guarantees, so a layer can reach past the project company to you. Banking: the senior lender will usually forbid any other debt or pledge without its consent. Governance: preferred investors commonly take consent rights over major decisions, which narrows what you can decide alone. Estate: if your interest sits in a holding company, the stack's control triggers can interact with what happens to that holding company on death or incapacity. Exit: each layer has its own prepayment terms, and every one of them must agree before you can refinance or sell cleanly.

Callback

In week 2 we learned inversion: instead of asking how a plan succeeds, ask how it fails. Apply that here. Write down the three events most likely to stop the project paying its junior layers on time, then trace, layer by layer, who gets the right to act first when each event happens. That exercise usually tells you more about a stack than its blended interest rate.

Recap

The capital stack is a repayment queue. Position sets the price, position sets who loses first, and the documents set who can take control and how fast. Size the stack to a downside value, read every layer's remedies, and never accept a junior layer the senior lender has not approved.

Next: Ford, with Roman, takes a real collapse through failure forensics: Stuyvesant Town and the stack built on a business plan.
checklist: Draw the stack with each layer as a percentage band of cost and of value
Price each layer and calculate the blended cost of capital
Calculate the value at which each layer above senior starts to lose
Read every layer's remedies and note which can take control fastest
Confirm the senior lender has approved every junior layer in writing
Test whether the asset's return exceeds the cost of each expensive layer
List every personal guarantee any layer is asking for
Run the Six-Lens Check before signing anything
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, here is the capital stack in one minute. It is a queue. Senior debt sits at the bottom, secured by a mortgage, repaid first and losing last. Above it, mezzanine debt, usually secured by a pledge of the shares in the owning company. Above that, preferred equity, which is promised its return before the ordinary owners. At the top, common equity: paid last, first to lose, keeps the upside. If a 100 million dollar project with 15 million of common equity loses 20 percent of its value, the common equity is gone. Position sets price, so the higher layers cost more. Position also sets control, and the surprise is that the junior layers can often move faster than the senior lender, because a share pledge or a removal right acts quicker than a mortgage enforcement. So I size the stack to a downside value, I read every layer's remedies, and I never add a layer the senior lender has not approved.
terms: Capital stack — the full set of debt and equity funding a project, arranged in the order each is repaid and each absorbs losses.
Mezzanine loan — a loan ranking behind the senior loan, commonly secured by a pledge of the ownership interests in the borrowing company rather than by the property itself.
Preferred equity — an ownership interest promised its return and capital ahead of common equity, usually with contractual rights to take control if those promises are missed.

hostile.q: Your stack goes to 85 percent of cost. At what value do your preferred investors take control, and why should I believe it will not happen?
hostile.a: Preferred equity starts to lose when value falls below 75 percent of cost, and its control right triggers on a missed payment or a missed completion date, not on value alone. Our downside case has value at 90 percent of cost and completion three months late, which still clears the pref payment from the funded reserve. I will show you the trigger table and the reserve schedule, and the intercreditor terms the senior lender has already approved.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman (Risk and the lender's view)
title: Stuyvesant Town: a capital stack built on a business plan
summary: In 2006 a record purchase of a large Manhattan rental community was funded with several layers of debt that the property's existing income could not pay. The plan relied on rents rising fast enough before the reserves ran out. They did not, and by early 2010 the owners walked away and the equity was gone.
body:
Stuyvesant Town is the clearest lesson in this course on what happens when a capital stack is sized to a business plan instead of to the income the property actually produces. The equity was lost, and the junior lenders fought over what remained.

Recall

Q. What is debt yield?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount. Unlike the coverage ratio it ignores the interest rate and amortisation, so it shows how much income backs each dollar of loan whatever the loan terms.

Q. What is a minute book, and why would a lender ask to see it?

A. The company's official record of its constitution, resolutions, directors and shareholders. A lender reads it to confirm the borrower exists, that the signatories have authority, and that the borrowing was properly approved.

Q. In a condominium, what does the buyer actually own?

A. Title to the individual unit plus a share in the common elements, governed by the condominium's declaration and bylaws.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the junior layers of a stack are only safe if the property can pay them. When a stack depends on income the property does not yet earn, the developer has quietly made a bet on the future and financed it with other people's money and a clock. This case shows how that bet unfolds. The facts below are the public outline as I understand it; verify the detail against reporting from the period before you quote any of it.

Step 1: Timeline

In late 2006 a joint venture led by Tishman Speyer and BlackRock agreed to buy Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village in Manhattan, a community of roughly eleven thousand apartments, for about 5.4 billion dollars, widely reported at the time as the largest residential property sale in American history. Most of the apartments were rent-stabilised, meaning rents were regulated and could rise only within legal limits. The purchase was funded with a senior mortgage, several layers of mezzanine debt and equity from large institutional investors, including public pension funds. In 2009 New York's highest court ruled in a tenants' case that owners who had taken a particular property tax benefit could not remove apartments from rent regulation in the way the owners had been doing. In early 2010 the owners defaulted and turned the property over to the lenders. The equity was lost. Years later, in 2015, the property was sold to new owners.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. First, paying a price that the existing rents could not support. Second, funding most of that price with debt, stacked in layers. Third, covering the gap between the property's income and its debt payments with reserve accounts funded at closing, which only buys time, not solvency.

Step 3: Assumptions

The underwriting assumed that a large share of regulated apartments would move to market rents quickly, as tenants left and units were renovated and re-let. It assumed the legal path to doing so was secure. And it assumed the property's market value would keep rising, so that any shortfall could be refinanced later against a higher value.

Step 4: Incentives

Each party was paid to say yes. Sponsors earn fees and a share of profits on a closed deal. Lenders who package senior loans into securities earn fees and pass on the risk. Mezzanine lenders earn a high coupon. Institutional investors had capital to deploy in a strong market. Nobody at the table was paid to say no.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The loudest sign was the plainest: on the day of purchase the property's net operating income did not cover the total debt service. The reserves existed precisely because everybody knew that. A second sign was regulatory: the conversion strategy depended on the rules about rent stabilisation, and those rules were being contested by tenants. A third was the market: credit was unusually loose in 2006, which is exactly when a reference class of highly levered purchases should make you more cautious, not less.

Say that out loud now.

Step 6: The point of no return

Ford's view is that the point of no return came at signing, not at default. Once the stack was built on a gap that only rent growth could close, the outcome depended on the speed of conversion versus the speed at which reserves were spent. When the court ruling slowed conversion and the financial crisis hit values, the reserves were simply a countdown. Roman adds the lender's lens: by 2009 the combined coverage ratio was nowhere near one, and no refinance was possible against the falling value.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was sizing the capital stack to projected income rather than in-place income. Everything else, the ruling, the crisis, the fights among creditors afterwards, was an event that a properly sized stack could have survived.

The applied lesson

Here is a worked check you can run on any deal, with hypothetical round numbers. Suppose a property earns 10 million dollars of net operating income today. Your stack requires 14 million a year of total debt service across senior and mezzanine. The shortfall is 4 million a year. If the reserve is 12 million, you have three years to raise income by at least 4 million, which is a 40 percent increase. Write that sentence down in plain words: we must raise income 40 percent in three years or lose the equity. If it sounds heroic said aloud, it is.

Second example. Run the same deal with a stack whose total debt service is 9 million. Current income covers it 1.11 times. There is no countdown. The business plan becomes upside instead of survival. The difference between the two stacks is not the interest rate; it is whether time works for you or against you.

What Roman would have asked

Roman sits in the lender's chair and asks four questions of any stack like this. First: what does the property earn today, not after the plan? Second: through which layer does today's income stop covering the payments? Third: if the plan runs at half speed, in which month does the reserve run out? Fourth: what outside event, legal, political or market, could stop the plan altogether, and who has studied it? In a case like Stuyvesant Town the answers would have been uncomfortable on all four counts. The point is not that the buyers failed to ask; it is that the answers did not change the decision. A rule that only produces a warning is not a control. A control is a threshold written down in advance that stops the deal, or shrinks the stack, when the answer crosses it. Write yours before you see the next attractive purchase, because once you have fallen for an asset you will find reasons to move the line.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is funding a gap with a reserve and calling it a margin of safety. A reserve sized to a hopeful timeline is a fuse. The control is to size every layer to in-place income, or to fund a reserve sized to the downside timeline, with a written test of what happens when that reserve is half spent.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner looks at the senior coverage ratio, sees comfort, and stops. The senior loan was not the problem in a stack like this. Calculate coverage through every layer that must be paid in cash, because that is the number that decides whether the equity survives.

Callback

In week 2 we met the outside view: before trusting your own forecast, ask how similar projects actually performed. A highly levered purchase priced on rent growth, closed at the top of a credit boom, belongs to a reference class with a poor record. The outside view was available on the day of signing, which is why Ford places the point of no return there.

Recap

A stack sized to a business plan is a bet with a countdown attached. Size to in-place income, compute coverage through every cash-pay layer, and treat a reserve as time bought, not risk removed.

Rule 37: I never size a capital stack to projected income; every cash-pay layer must be covered by in-place income or by a reserve sized to the downside timeline.

Next: Priya on the money: what each layer costs, and how mezzanine and preferred equity change the common investor's return.
checklist: State in-place net operating income separately from projected income
Calculate coverage through every cash-pay layer, not just the senior loan
Size any reserve to the downside timeline and write what happens when it is half spent
Identify every legal or regulatory assumption the business plan depends on
Name who at the table is paid to say no
Write the required income growth as one plain sentence and say it aloud
Check where the market sits in the credit cycle before adding leverage

In late 2006 a joint venture bought a Manhattan rental community of about eleven thousand mostly rent-regulated apartments for roughly 5.4 billion dollars, funded with a senior mortgage, several mezzanine layers and institutional equity. The income on day one did not cover the debt payments, so reserves filled the gap while the owners tried to move units to market rents. terms: In-place income — the net operating income a property actually produces today under existing leases, before any planned improvement.
Interest reserve — cash set aside at closing to pay debt service while income is too low to cover it.
Rent stabilisation — a form of rent regulation that limits how fast and how far rents on covered apartments may rise.

hostile.q: Your total debt service exceeds today's income. Why is this not Stuyvesant Town?
hostile.a: Because the gap is covered by a reserve sized to our downside timeline, not our base case, and the plan does not depend on a legal change or a refinance at a higher value. If leasing runs at half our assumed pace, the reserve still lasts until stabilised income covers debt service through the mezzanine layer. I will show you the month at which the reserve would be half spent and what we do at that point.

rule: Rule 37: I never size a capital stack to projected income; every cash-pay layer must be covered by in-place income or by a reserve sized to the downside timeline.

title: What each layer costs, and what it does to your return
summary: Junior capital lets a developer put in less equity, but it costs more and it magnifies both gains and losses. This lesson works through the same project funded two ways and shows when mezzanine helps the common equity and when it quietly hurts it.
body:
Adding mezzanine or preferred equity is a trade: less of your own money in, more cost and more volatility on what remains. It improves the common equity's return only when the property earns more than the junior layer costs.

Recall

Q. In the Stuyvesant Town case, what was the root cause?

A. The capital stack was sized to projected income rather than to the income the property actually earned, so a reserve had to cover the gap while the business plan played out.

Q. What is signing authority, and where is it recorded?

A. The power of a named person to bind the company to a contract, recorded in the company's resolutions and minute book.

Q. In a hotel, what does gross operating profit measure?

A. Revenue minus the hotel's operating expenses at the property level, before management fees, fixed charges and capital reserves.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the most common pitch for junior capital is that it lets you do a bigger project, or keep more of the upside, with less of your own cash. That pitch is half true. The other half is that you have bought a more expensive layer of risk and placed it directly under your own money. You need to be able to calculate, quickly and honestly, which half dominates on a given deal.

Leverage cuts both ways

In plain English, borrowing magnifies results. If the asset does well, your smaller slice of equity earns more per dollar. If it does badly, your smaller slice is wiped out sooner. Professionals call the good case positive leverage and the bad case negative leverage, and the dividing line is simple: when the property's yield on cost is higher than the cost of the borrowed layer, leverage helps; when it is lower, leverage hurts the cash yield.

Worked example one, with hypothetical round numbers. A project costs 100 million dollars and earns stabilised net operating income of 7 million, a 7 percent yield on cost. Stack A has a senior loan of 60 million at 6 percent interest-only and common equity of 40 million. Stack B has the same senior loan, a mezzanine loan of 15 million at 12 percent interest-only, and common equity of 25 million.

LineStack AStack B
Net operating income7.00 million7.00 million
Senior interest at 6 percent3.60 million3.60 million
Mezzanine interest at 12 percentnone1.80 million
Cash to common equity3.40 million1.60 million
Cash yield on common equity8.5 percent6.4 percent

The mezzanine costs 12 percent and the property earns 7, so every mezzanine dollar loses money on a cash basis. The common equity is 15 million smaller, but its annual cash yield fell from 8.5 percent to 6.4 percent.

Where junior capital earns its keep

Mezzanine pays off on value growth, not on cash flow. Worked example two uses the same two stacks at sale. If the building sells for 120 million, Stack A's equity receives 60 million on 40 invested, a gain of 50 percent. Stack B's equity receives 45 million on 25 invested, a gain of 80 percent. If instead the building sells for 90 million, Stack A's equity receives 30 on 40, a loss of 25 percent, while Stack B's receives 15 on 25, a loss of 40 percent. Same building, same market, different stack: the junior layer widened the range of outcomes in both directions.

So the professional question is never simply whether mezzanine raises the return. It is whether the extra expected gain is worth the extra spread of outcomes, and whether the project can carry the higher cash cost in the years before value is realised.

Say that out loud now.

Preferred equity and the blended cost

Preferred equity often accrues its return rather than paying it in cash, which protects near-term cash flow but compounds a growing claim ahead of the common equity. If a hypothetical 10 million of preferred equity accrues at 10 percent a year for three years, it is owed about 13.3 million at the end, before the common investors see a dollar. Compounding is quiet, and it is the reason a deal that looked fine at year one can leave little for the common equity at year four.

The blended cost of capital is the average cost of all the layers, weighted by size. In Stack B, ignoring equity, the debt alone blends to 60 at 6 and 15 at 12, or 7.2 percent on 75 million. That number is now higher than the 7 percent yield on cost, which is the early warning that the debt is more expensive, on average, than what the building earns.

The true cost is more than the coupon

Junior lenders are paid in more than interest. A mezzanine term sheet commonly carries an origination fee charged at closing, an exit fee charged at repayment, and sometimes a minimum return, meaning a guaranteed multiple of interest even if you repay early. Worked example: a hypothetical 15 million mezzanine loan at 12 percent with a 1 percent fee in and a 1 percent fee out, repaid after two years. Interest is 3.6 million, fees are 300,000, so total cost is 3.9 million over two years, or about 1.95 million a year, which is 13 percent of the loan, not 12. If the term sheet adds a minimum of 18 months of interest and you refinance at month 12, you pay six months of interest for money you no longer hold. Always convert every fee into an annual percentage over the realistic holding period before comparing offers. These fee structures are commercial practice, negotiated deal by deal, not fixed standards.

How the best do it

Experienced sponsors tend to test every proposed junior layer against a simple pair of questions: does the property's yield on cost exceed the layer's all-in cost, including fees, and if not, is the expected value gain large and near enough to justify negative carry? They also model the payoff with value flat, not only with value rising. A small developer can copy both habits on one page.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. Your common equity in a levered project is the most volatile line you own, because it sits at the top of the queue. A deal funded with junior capital may also show up as a contingent liability, because mezzanine lenders often ask the sponsor for guarantees. List those guarantees on your personal balance sheet beside the equity, at the amount you could be called on, not at zero. And notice concentration: the smaller the equity cheque, the more tempting it is to do several such deals at once, which can raise your total exposure to one market while each deal looks small.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is negative carry that outlasts your patience: paying a junior layer more than the property earns for longer than planned, while accrued preferred returns compound ahead of you. The control is a two-line test on every deal: cash yield to common equity with value flat, and the number of months the project can sustain negative carry before it must sell or refinance.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares projected returns only in the upside case. A junior layer always looks brilliant when value rises. Compare the stacks at value flat and value down by ten percent, and you will see what you are actually buying.

Callback

Back in week 15 we learned that internal rate of return can flatter a deal, especially when cash comes back early or leverage is high. Mezzanine is a common way to inflate a projected return while increasing risk. When you see a high equity return, ask what the return would be unlevered, and how much of the gap is borrowed volatility.

Recap

Junior capital is expensive leverage. It helps when the asset earns more than it costs or when value grows, and it hurts the cash yield and deepens the losses when neither happens. Test every layer with value flat, track accruing claims, and record guarantees on your own balance sheet.

Next: LEX on the rules: the intercreditor agreement, subordination, and how Canada and Guyana approach security over shares.
checklist: Compare yield on cost with each junior layer's all-in cost including fees
Calculate cash yield to common equity with value flat
Run the sale case at value up, flat and down ten percent
Project accrued preferred return at the planned exit year
Calculate the blended cost of the debt layers against yield on cost
Count the months of negative carry the project can sustain
List every guarantee on your personal balance sheet at its callable amount
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, junior capital in sixty seconds. Mezzanine and preferred equity let you put in less of your own cash, but they cost more and they magnify both gains and losses. Take a hypothetical 100 million dollar project earning 7 percent on cost. Fund it 60 senior at 6 percent and 40 equity, and the equity yields 8.5 percent in cash. Replace 15 of that equity with mezzanine at 12 percent, and the equity yield drops to 6.4 percent, because every mezzanine dollar costs more than the building earns. At a sale for 120, the mezzanine stack gives the equity 80 percent instead of 50. At a sale for 90, it loses 40 percent instead of 25. Junior capital earns its keep through value growth, not cash flow. So I test every layer at value flat, I track accruing preferred returns, and I list every guarantee on my own balance sheet.
terms: Positive leverage — borrowing at a cost below the asset's yield, which raises the return on equity.
Negative carry — paying more on a layer of capital than the asset earns on that money, which drains cash each period.
Blended cost of capital — the average cost of all funding layers, weighted by the size of each.

hostile.q: Your mezzanine costs more than the building yields. Why are you paying it?
hostile.a: Because without it we would need 15 million more equity we do not want to commit to one asset. We accept the negative carry for a defined period: our model shows the project can sustain it for 30 months with value flat, and stabilised value creates a refinance that retires the mezzanine at month 24 in the base case. If value is flat at month 24, we still cover all interest from income and reserve, and we lose return, not the asset.

title: The intercreditor agreement: the rules between lenders
summary: When a project has a senior loan and a mezzanine loan, the two lenders sign a contract between themselves that decides who may act, when, and with whose consent. This lesson teaches the clauses that matter to the developer, and compares in concept how Canada and Guyana approach security over shares.
body:
The intercreditor agreement is the contract that keeps two lenders from destroying the project while they protect themselves. You are usually not a party to it, but it decides what happens to you.

Recall

Q. When does mezzanine debt help the common equity's return?

A. When the property earns more than the mezzanine costs, or when value grows enough to outweigh the negative carry; otherwise it lowers the cash yield and deepens losses.

Q. What is a resolution, in company law terms?

A. A formal decision of the directors or shareholders, recorded in writing, that authorises the company to act, such as borrowing or signing a loan.

Q. What is a condominium declaration?

A. The registered document that creates the condominium, defines the units and common elements, and sets out the owners' shares and the rules that bind them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, two lenders with claims on the same project have opposite instincts in a crisis. The senior lender wants to protect its position, often by stopping funding or enforcing early. The mezzanine lender wants time and the chance to rescue its investment. Without rules between them, each could undo the other's remedies and the project would be stuck. The intercreditor agreement sets those rules before anyone is under stress. Lending terms and market practice vary, and the clauses below are commercial practice, not standards set by any code. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law of each loan.

Subordination, two ways

In plain English, subordination means agreeing to stand behind someone else. There are two kinds. Contractual subordination is a promise in writing: the junior lender agrees it will not be paid, or will not enforce, until the senior lender's conditions are met. Structural subordination arises from how the companies are arranged. If the senior lender lends to the company that owns the building, and the mezzanine lender lends to the parent company above it, the mezzanine lender is automatically behind every creditor of the building company, because the parent only receives what the building company has left over.

Most mezzanine deals use both. The structure puts the mezzanine lender one level up, and the intercreditor agreement then spells out exactly what each lender may do.

The clauses that matter to you

Professionally, a developer reads an intercreditor agreement for six things. First, payment: whether the mezzanine lender may receive interest while the senior loan is current, and whether its payments stop when the senior loan defaults. Second, the standstill: a period during which one lender must not enforce while the other tries to fix the problem. Third, cure rights: the mezzanine lender's right to pay overdue senior interest or fix a covenant breach to prevent senior enforcement. Fourth, a purchase option: the mezzanine lender's right to buy the senior loan, usually at par, if the senior lender starts to enforce. Fifth, the qualified transferee test: the list of who may step in and own the project if the mezzanine lender enforces, often defined by experience and net worth. Sixth, modification limits: caps on how far either lender may change its own loan, such as increasing the amount or the rate, without the other's consent.

Worked example one. A hypothetical project misses a senior interest payment of 400,000 dollars because lease-up is slow. Without a cure right, the senior lender could declare a default and accelerate. With a cure right, the mezzanine lender pays the 400,000, adds it to what it is owed, and the senior loan is current again. The developer keeps the project for now, but the mezzanine claim has just grown, and many intercreditors limit how many times cures may be used.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two. The mezzanine loan defaults. The mezzanine lender enforces its share pledge and becomes the owner of the borrowing company. That is a change of control, which the senior loan normally prohibits. The intercreditor agreement is what says this particular change of control is permitted, provided the new owner is a qualified transferee and replaces any guarantees. For the developer, this means a mezzanine default can remove you entirely, quickly, while the senior loan carries on undisturbed.

Preferred equity is different

A preferred equity investor is an owner, not a lender, so there is usually no intercreditor agreement. Its rights live in the partnership or operating agreement, and the senior lender may ask for a recognition agreement confirming that a change of manager triggered by the preferred investor will not breach the senior loan. Read both documents together, because the senior lender's consent is what makes the preferred investor's removal right actually work.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source for both countries before relying on it. In Canada, the common law provinces register security over shares and other personal property under provincial personal property security legislation, with a public registry that sets priority largely by registration, while Quebec follows its own civil law framework. Land mortgages are registered in each province's land titles or registry system. Guyana's legal system is founded on the common law, with land registered under its own deeds and land registration systems. For a share pledge in Guyana, the questions to ask counsel are whether a modern registry for security over shares and movable property exists, how priority between competing claims is set, and how quickly and through which forum a pledge can be enforced. The concept is the same in both places: a junior lender's real position depends on how its security is perfected and enforced, not on the label in the term sheet.

What to ask your lawyer to fight for

Even though you will not sign the intercreditor agreement, your lawyer can press both lenders, because each needs you to close. Three requests matter most. Ask that the standstill be long enough to raise new equity, measured against how long that genuinely takes you, not against market habit. Ask that the qualified transferee test require real experience operating this asset type, so that the party who could replace you is competent to finish the building, which protects the senior lender too. And ask that cure payments made by the mezzanine lender do not automatically become new default triggers under your own loan. A fourth, often overlooked, is notice: make sure every default notice that either lender sends to the other is copied to you at the same time. You cannot fix what you do not know about, and some intercreditor agreements let lenders talk to each other about your default before you have been told. Your lawyer's instructions should list these points in writing, so the advice comes back against each one.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is signing your loan documents before the intercreditor terms are settled, so the two lenders later agree rules that suit them and not the project, such as a short standstill or a broad qualified transferee definition that lets almost anyone take your place. The control is to make an agreed intercreditor term sheet a condition of your own closing and to have your lawyer review it, even though you will not sign it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the senior lender is the threat and the mezzanine lender is a friend. In a default, the mezzanine lender may be the party with the fastest route to owning your company. Read its enforcement path first.

Callback

In week 20 we learned that conditions and remedies, not the headline price, decide what a contract really does. The intercreditor agreement is that lesson applied to lenders: the payment blockage, the standstill and the cure rights are conditions and remedies, and together they decide whether a bad quarter becomes a lost company.

Recap

Subordination can be contractual or structural, and mezzanine deals usually use both. Read the intercreditor agreement for payments, standstill, cure rights, purchase option, the qualified transferee test and modification limits. Preferred equity lives in the partnership agreement and needs the senior lender's recognition to bite.

Next: Priya with the numbers: building a capital stack step by step, from attachment points to coverage through every layer.
checklist: Map which company each lender lends to, to see structural subordination
Read the payment blockage terms for the mezzanine loan
Note the length and trigger of every standstill period
Read the cure rights and any limit on how often they may be used
Read the qualified transferee definition as if a stranger will use it
Check the caps on increasing either loan without consent
Confirm a recognition agreement exists for any preferred equity removal right
Professional sign-off required: lawyer qualified in each governing law
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the intercreditor agreement in sixty seconds. When a project has a senior loan and a mezzanine loan, the two lenders sign a contract between themselves. Subordination comes two ways: by contract, a written promise to stand behind, and by structure, when the mezzanine lender lends one company up and only receives what the building company has left. I read six clauses: when the mezzanine may be paid, the standstill before anyone enforces, the mezzanine's cure rights, its option to buy the senior loan, the qualified transferee test for who may take over, and the caps on changing either loan. A mezzanine default can hand my company to a qualified transferee while the senior loan carries on. Preferred equity has no intercreditor; its rights live in the partnership agreement and need the senior lender's recognition. I make settled intercreditor terms a condition of my closing.
terms: Contractual subordination — a written agreement by one creditor to be paid or to enforce only after another creditor's conditions are met.
Standstill — an agreed period during which a creditor may not enforce while another party attempts to cure a default.
Qualified transferee — the class of parties, usually defined by experience and net worth, permitted to take ownership of the borrower if a junior lender enforces.

hostile.q: You are not a party to the intercreditor agreement. Why should your lawyer review it at all?
hostile.a: Because it decides how fast I can lose the company. The standstill, the cure rights and the qualified transferee definition set the timetable and the identity of who replaces me. I make an agreed intercreditor term sheet a condition of my closing so that the rules are fixed before I commit equity, and I want my counsel to confirm they leave time to fix a problem before anyone enforces.

title: Building a stack step by step: bands, coverage and the downside
summary: A worked calculation that builds a hypothetical four-layer capital stack from cost and income, finds where each layer sits, calculates coverage through every cash-pay layer, and then shows who loses what in a downside case.
body:
You can test any capital stack with four calculations: the band each layer occupies, its cost, coverage through every cash-pay layer, and who loses what when value falls. Do them in that order and the weak layer shows itself.

Recall

Q. What is a standstill in an intercreditor agreement?

A. An agreed period during which one lender may not enforce while the other attempts to cure the default.

Q. What is an officer's certificate, and why does a lender want one at closing?

A. A signed statement by a company officer confirming facts such as the accuracy of the constitutional documents and the authority of the signatories, so the lender can rely on them.

Q. What is average daily rate in a hotel?

A. Room revenue divided by the number of rooms sold over the period.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a term sheet arrives with an interest rate and a loan amount. It does not arrive with the answer to the only question that matters to you: how much can go wrong before you lose control or lose money. You calculate that yourself, and it takes about fifteen minutes once you know the steps.

Step 1: Set out the stack and its bands

Hypothetical project: total development cost 50,000,000 dollars. Funding:

  • Senior loan: 30,000,000 dollars, interest-only at 6 percent
  • Mezzanine loan: 7,500,000 dollars, interest-only at 12 percent
  • Preferred equity: 5,000,000 dollars, 10 percent return, paid in cash
  • Common equity: 7,500,000 dollars

Check the total: 30 plus 7.5 plus 5 plus 7.5 equals 50 million. Now express each as a band of cost. The point at which a layer starts to lose money is its attachment point; the point at which it is wiped out entirely is its detachment point. Senior occupies 0 to 60 percent, because 30 divided by 50 is 0.60. Mezzanine occupies 60 to 75 percent, adding 7.5 divided by 50, which is 0.15. Preferred occupies 75 to 85 percent. Common occupies 85 to 100 percent.

Step 2: Price each cash-pay layer

Annual cash cost, in dollars per year:

  • Senior: 30,000,000 times 0.06 equals 1,800,000
  • Mezzanine: 7,500,000 times 0.12 equals 900,000
  • Preferred: 5,000,000 times 0.10 equals 500,000

Cumulative cash cost: 1,800,000 through senior, 2,700,000 through mezzanine, 3,200,000 through preferred. These rates are hypothetical; actual pricing is commercial practice that moves with the market.

Step 3: Coverage through every layer

Stabilised net operating income is 3,500,000 dollars a year. Divide it by each cumulative cost:

  • Through senior: 3,500,000 divided by 1,800,000 equals 1.94 times
  • Through mezzanine: 3,500,000 divided by 2,700,000 equals 1.30 times
  • Through preferred: 3,500,000 divided by 3,200,000 equals 1.09 times

The senior figure looks very safe. The figure that decides whether the common equity receives anything is the last one, and 1.09 means income can fall only about 8.5 percent before the preferred return is no longer covered in cash. That figure, the cumulative coverage ratio, is the second term for today.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Break-even income for each layer

Break-even is the income at which coverage equals exactly 1.00. For the mezzanine layer it is 2,700,000 dollars. The drop from 3,500,000 to 2,700,000 is 800,000, which is 800,000 divided by 3,500,000, or about 22.9 percent. So income can fall roughly 23 percent before the mezzanine is in cash difficulty, but only about 8.5 percent before the preferred return is. State both in a sentence.

Step 5: Value and loan-to-value at stabilisation

Value the stabilised building at a hypothetical 6.5 percent capitalisation rate: 3,500,000 divided by 0.065 equals about 53,850,000 dollars. Loan-to-value through the mezzanine layer: 37,500,000 divided by 53,850,000 equals about 69.6 percent. Through preferred: 42,500,000 divided by 53,850,000 equals about 78.9 percent.

Step 6: The downside waterfall of losses

Now the second worked example. Suppose the market moves and the building is valued at a 7.5 percent capitalisation rate on income that has fallen 10 percent to 3,150,000. Value is 3,150,000 divided by 0.075, which equals 42,000,000 dollars. Allocate it from the bottom up:

LayerClaimRecoveredLoss
Senior30,000,00030,000,0000
Mezzanine7,500,0007,500,0000
Preferred5,000,0004,500,000500,000
Common7,500,00007,500,000

A 10 percent income fall plus a one-point move in capitalisation rate removed 22 percent of value, from 53.85 to 42 million, and erased the common equity entirely. Coverage through preferred in this case is 3,150,000 divided by 3,200,000, or 0.98: the preferred return can no longer be paid in cash, which in many deals is exactly the trigger for removing the developer.

Step 7: Write the conclusion

One paragraph: the stack is safe for the senior and mezzanine lenders under this downside, the preferred investor takes a small loss and gains a control trigger, and the common equity is wiped out. The fix options are a smaller preferred layer, a cash-pay preferred converted to accruing, a larger common cushion, or a lower purchase price.

Step 8: Test the fix

A finding is only useful if you test the cure. Rework the stack with a smaller preferred layer and a larger common cushion: senior 30,000,000, mezzanine 7,500,000, preferred 2,500,000 at 10 percent, common 10,000,000. The total is still 50,000,000. Preferred now occupies 75 to 80 percent of cost and common 80 to 100.

Cumulative cash cost through preferred becomes 2,700,000 plus 250,000, which equals 2,950,000 dollars a year. Coverage through preferred at stabilised income: 3,500,000 divided by 2,950,000 equals 1.19 times, up from 1.09. Income can now fall about 15.7 percent, calculated as 550,000 divided by 3,500,000, before the preferred return is uncovered.

Rerun the downside at 42,000,000 dollars of value. Senior takes 30,000,000, mezzanine 7,500,000, preferred its full 2,500,000, for 40,000,000 in total. Common recovers 2,000,000 of its 10,000,000. Downside coverage through preferred is 3,150,000 divided by 2,950,000, or 1.07, so the preferred return is still paid in cash and its control trigger does not fire.

The price of that safety is your own money: common equity rose from 7.5 to 10 million. Whether that is worth it is a judgment, but now it is an informed one, expressed in dollars and in coverage, not in adjectives.

What the lender will recompute

Do not expect a lender to accept your figures. Its credit team will rebuild Steps 3 to 6 from its own inputs: its own appraiser's capitalisation rate, its own view of achievable rent, and often a stressed interest rate rather than the coupon. Expect its coverage figures to be lower than yours. The useful habit is to run the lender's likely inputs yourself before you submit, so that the first version of the number it sees is one you have already explained. If your stack only works on your own optimistic inputs, you will find out in credit committee, at the worst possible moment.

Units and checks

Three habits keep this work honest. Keep every figure in the same unit, dollars per year for income and cost, dollars for claims and value, and percentages only as ratios of two of those. Check each table adds to the total before reading anything into it. And round only at the end; rounding the capitalisation rate or the coverage early can move the answer by enough to change a decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting senior coverage as the safety figure when the control trigger sits in a junior layer. The control is to show cumulative coverage and break-even income for every cash-pay layer on the first page of every financing memo.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner tests the downside by moving one input. Real downsides move income and capitalisation rate together. Always move both.

Callback

In week 10 we defined the capitalisation rate as income divided by value. Step 6 shows why a one-point change matters so much: at these levels it moves value by about 13 percent on its own, and in a levered stack that change lands entirely on the top layers.

Recap

Bands, cost, cumulative coverage, break-even, value, then the downside waterfall of losses. The weak layer is the one with the thinnest coverage and the nearest control trigger, and it is rarely the senior loan.

Next: Priya in the room: negotiating a mezzanine term sheet without giving away control.
checklist: Check the stack adds to total cost
Express each layer as a band of cost and of value
Calculate annual cash cost for each cash-pay layer
Calculate cumulative coverage through every layer
Calculate break-even income and the percentage drop for each layer
Run a downside that moves income and capitalisation rate together
Allocate the downside value from the bottom up
Write the conclusion and the fix options in one paragraph
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, testing a stack in sixty seconds. A hypothetical 50 million dollar project: 30 senior at 6 percent, 7.5 mezzanine at 12, 5 preferred at 10, 7.5 common. Bands: senior 0 to 60 percent, mezzanine 60 to 75, preferred 75 to 85, common 85 to 100. Annual cost: 1.8 million, then 2.7 cumulative, then 3.2. With income of 3.5 million, coverage is 1.94 through senior but only 1.09 through preferred, so income can fall about 8.5 percent before the preferred return is uncovered. Now the downside: income down 10 percent and the cap rate up a point, from 6.5 to 7.5. Value falls from about 53.85 to 42 million. Senior and mezzanine are whole, preferred loses half a million and gets its control trigger, and common is wiped out. The weak layer is the one with the thinnest coverage, and it is rarely the senior loan.
terms: Attachment point — the level of value, as a percentage of cost or value, below which a layer of capital begins to lose money.
Cumulative coverage ratio — net operating income divided by the combined annual cash cost of a layer and every layer senior to it.
Break-even income — the net operating income at which a layer's cumulative coverage equals exactly one.

hostile.q: Your senior coverage is nearly two times. Why is your preferred investor nervous?
hostile.a: Because coverage through the preferred layer is 1.09, so a drop in income of about 8.5 percent leaves its return uncovered in cash, and in our downside, with income down 10 percent and the cap rate up a point, it takes a small loss and gains the right to replace me. That is why we are proposing to make the preferred return accrue for the first two years and to increase the common equity cushion.

title: In the room with a mezzanine lender
summary: A realistic negotiation with a mezzanine lender over the terms that decide control: the cure period, the guarantee and the default triggers. What to say, what never to say, the question behind the question, and how to hold steady when the lender pushes.
body:
A mezzanine negotiation is not mainly about the interest rate. It is about how much time you get to fix a problem before the lender can take your company, and the lender knows that better than you do.

Recall

Q. In the worked stack, why was coverage through preferred the number that mattered?

A. Because it was the thinnest coverage, 1.09 times, so a small fall in income uncovered the preferred return and could trigger the investor's control rights.

Q. What does a shareholders' or operating agreement typically control that a lender's documents do not?

A. How the owners make decisions among themselves, fund the company, transfer interests and replace the manager.

Q. In a mixed-use building, why do lenders often value each use separately?

A. Because each use, residential, retail or hotel, carries different income risk and trades at a different capitalisation rate.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the mezzanine lender you meet will have negotiated hundreds of these. Some lend to earn a coupon; some lend hoping to own. Your job is to find out which, without giving away terms you will need in a bad year. The scene below is hypothetical.

The scene

A hypothetical 60 million dollar residential project. The senior lender has committed 36 million. You need 9 million of mezzanine. Across the table is the mezzanine lender's managing director and its counsel. The term sheet offers 9 million at a high coupon, a pledge of the shares in your project company, a full repayment guarantee from you personally, a 10-day cure period, and a default if completion slips more than 30 days past the scheduled date.

The managing director opens: "Our rate is firm. Everything else is standard."

The lines to say

"Thank you. I accept the rate is your price. I want to spend our time on the three terms that decide whether a delay becomes a default."

"The completion date: our schedule has 60 days of contingency inside it already, and our senior lender allows 120 days. Can we align with the senior loan, so one event does not trigger two different clocks?"

"The guarantee: I can offer a completion guarantee and a carve-out guarantee for fraud and wilful misconduct. I will not offer a full repayment guarantee on a loan priced as equity-like risk. What would you need to see to accept that?"

"The cure period: 10 days does not let us raise additional equity or close a cure. We are asking for 30 days for monetary defaults and 60 for non-monetary ones, with the right to cure by contributing cash."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

"We will never miss a date." It invites the lender to price your optimism into tighter triggers, and it is not true of any construction project.

"Whatever is standard is fine." There is no standard. Every term is a choice, and saying this hands all of them to the other side.

"We really need this closed by month end." The moment the lender knows your deadline, every remaining term gets harder.

The question behind the question

When the lender says "Why should we accept a longer cure period?", the real question is "Are you the kind of sponsor who will fix problems or hide them?" Answer that one: "Because we report monthly, we will tell you about a slip at the first sign, and a longer cure period lets us fix it instead of fighting you. Short cure periods turn early warnings into silence."

When the lender says "Who else is in the stack?", the real question is "Who will fight us in a default?" Answer it directly and offer the intercreditor term sheet the senior lender has already agreed.

Worked example: trading terms

Suppose the lender refuses the longer completion date but softens on the guarantee. Value each trade in time and dollars. A full repayment guarantee on 9 million exposes your personal balance sheet to 9 million plus interest. A 30-day completion trigger, against a schedule whose realistic slip is 60 to 90 days, has a meaningful chance of firing. Which is worse depends on your liquidity, but notice that a completion trigger costs you the company, while a guarantee costs you money. Many sponsors would rather give a capped guarantee than accept a hair trigger.

A second worked example: the lender asks for a cash sweep, meaning all surplus cash goes to repay the mezzanine after the senior is paid. On a building throwing off a hypothetical 600,000 dollars a year after senior debt service, a full sweep retires the loan faster but leaves nothing for reserves or the common equity. A counter of a 50 percent sweep, with the rest building a reserve, protects both.

The second half of the scene

The managing director comes back: "We can do 90 days on completion, 20-day cure on money defaults, 45 on everything else, and we will take a completion guarantee plus carve-outs, capped at 3 million, if you add a 1 percent exit fee."

You now have a real offer. Do not accept it in the room. Say: "That is a serious move, and I appreciate it. I want to check the 90 days against our schedule risk and the exit fee against our refinance timing. I will confirm by Friday." That line, from week 6, buys you the one thing you cannot get under pressure: time to calculate.

Back at your desk, run the numbers. The exit fee on 9 million is 90,000 dollars, about 1 percent, a cost you can model exactly. The 90-day completion buffer against a schedule whose realistic slip is 60 to 90 days is still tight; you might counter at 120 days in exchange for accepting the exit fee. The 3 million cap on the guarantee is something you measure against your own liquidity, not against the lender's comfort.

When you reply, put every agreed point in writing in one email, in the same order as the term sheet, and end with the one item still open. A written summary prevents the most common source of later disputes in financing: two parties remembering the same meeting differently.

Before you send that email, have your lawyer read the revised terms against the senior loan and the intercreditor term sheet. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the governing law of the mezzanine loan. A trigger that looks aligned in a term sheet can be misaligned in the drafting.

When to stay silent

After you name the term you want and the reason, stop. Let the lender respond. The urge to fill silence with a concession is strongest exactly when the other side is thinking about agreeing.

Holding your state

When counsel says "That is off-market," breathe out slowly, keep your voice low and your pace slow, and ask "Which recent deal are you comparing it to?" You are not arguing; you are asking for evidence. If you feel your jaw tighten, write the term down and say "Let me come back to that," then move on.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is winning the rate and losing the triggers. The control is to rank the terms before the meeting by how quickly each one can cost you control, and to negotiate them in that order.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates every clause with equal energy and runs out of goodwill before reaching the cure period. Spend your capital on the clauses that decide time and control.

Callback

In week 6 we learned to handle hostile questions by acknowledging, bridging and answering. "That is off-market" is a hostile question. Acknowledge it, bridge to what the term protects, and answer with your monthly reporting and your schedule contingency.

Recap

Accept the price, fight for time: align completion triggers with the senior loan, cap the guarantee, lengthen cure periods, soften any cash sweep. Never volunteer a deadline, never say "standard is fine", and stay quiet after your ask.

Next: Kema reviews the week: six questions, a Red Pen drill on a stack summary, and a two-minute boardroom explanation.
checklist: Rank the term sheet clauses by how fast each can cost control
Align every completion and default trigger with the senior loan
Offer a capped or carve-out guarantee instead of full repayment
Ask for monetary and non-monetary cure periods with a cash cure right
Counter any full cash sweep with a split to reserves
Bring the agreed senior intercreditor term sheet to the meeting
Never disclose your closing deadline
After each ask, stop talking and wait
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the mezzanine room in sixty seconds. The rate is their price; the triggers are where you live or die. I open by accepting the rate and naming the three terms that decide whether a delay becomes a default. I ask to align the completion trigger with the senior loan, so one slip does not start two clocks. I offer a completion and carve-out guarantee, not a full repayment guarantee. I ask for 30-day cure on money defaults and 60 on others, with the right to cure in cash. I never say we will never miss a date, never say standard is fine, and never reveal my deadline. When they ask why they should give a longer cure, the real question is whether I will hide problems, so I answer with monthly reporting. After each ask I stop and wait. Win the triggers, not the rate.
terms: Cure period — the time allowed after a default notice to remedy the default before the lender may enforce.
Cash sweep — a requirement that surplus cash flow be applied to repay a loan rather than distributed or reserved.
Completion guarantee — a sponsor's promise to a lender to finish the project and pay any cost overruns, as distinct from guaranteeing repayment of the whole loan.

hostile.q: If you are confident in your schedule, why do you need a 120-day completion buffer?
hostile.a: Because confidence is not a schedule. Our schedule carries 60 days of contingency, and the reference class for projects of this type shows slips beyond that are common. Aligning with the senior loan's 120 days means one delay triggers one conversation, not two defaults. In exchange, you get monthly reporting and immediate notice of any slip.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 37 review: the capital stack
summary: Six questions on the capital stack, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical financing summary with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: every layer of capital has a place in the queue, a price that follows from that place, and a route to control that the documents define. You should now be able to test any stack in fifteen minutes.

Recall

Q. What is the attachment point of a layer?

A. The level of value, as a percentage, below which that layer starts to lose money.

Q. What does sizing a loan to the binding limit mean?

A. Calculating the loan permitted by each of the lender's tests, such as coverage, debt yield and loan-to-value, and taking the smallest, because that test binds.

Q. What is a mixed-use building's biggest valuation trap?

A. Applying one capitalisation rate to all uses, when each use carries different risk and should be valued on its own terms.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, reviewing is how a week becomes a habit. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why does common equity lose first? Answer: Because it is repaid last. When value falls, losses consume the capital stack from the top down, and common equity sits at the top.

Question 2. Why can a mezzanine lender take control faster than the senior lender? Answer: Because it is commonly secured by a pledge of the shares in the borrowing company, which can often be enforced faster than a mortgage over real property, and taking the company brings the building with it.

Question 3. When does mezzanine debt help the common equity? Answer: When the property earns more than the mezzanine costs, or when value growth outweighs the negative carry. Otherwise it lowers cash yield and deepens losses.

Question 4. Name four clauses you read in an intercreditor agreement. Answer: Payment blockage, standstill, cure rights and the qualified transferee definition; also the purchase option and limits on modifying either loan.

Question 5. In the worked stack, why was 1.09 the important coverage figure? Answer: Because it was the cumulative coverage through preferred equity, the thinnest, so an income fall of about 8.5 percent uncovered the preferred return and could trigger its control rights.

Question 6. What was Rule 37? Answer: Never size a capital stack to projected income; every cash-pay layer must be covered by in-place income or by a reserve sized to the downside timeline.

Say that out loud now.

Week recap

Day 1 built the queue: senior, mezzanine, preferred, common, each with a band, a price and a remedy. Day 2 took Stuyvesant Town apart and found its root cause in sizing debt to a business plan. Day 3 showed that junior capital magnifies outcomes and only helps when the asset outearns it. Day 4 read the intercreditor agreement. Day 5 tested a stack in seven steps. Day 6 negotiated the triggers, not the rate.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical financing summary and find the defects before reading on.

Project cost 40 million. Senior loan 24 million, 60 percent loan-to-cost. Mezzanine 8 million. Preferred equity 4 million, which we count as equity for loan-to-value purposes. Total leverage therefore 32 million, or 80 percent. Net operating income 2.8 million against senior debt service of 1.44 million gives coverage of 1.94, which is very safe. Mezzanine pledge to be documented after closing. Intercreditor terms to be negotiated between the lenders. Reserve of 1 million covers any shortfall.

The defects. First, the arithmetic: 24 plus 8 is 32, but the preferred equity, which is promised its return and capital ahead of common, should be shown in the stack, taking total senior-to-preferred claims to 36 million, or 90 percent. Calling it equity hides 10 percent of cost. Second, coverage is shown through senior only. With mezzanine at, say, 12 percent, adding 960,000 a year, cumulative coverage through mezzanine is 2.8 divided by 2.4, or about 1.17, a very different story. Third, the mezzanine pledge documented after closing breaches the principle that every junior layer is approved before closing. Fourth, intercreditor terms left to the lenders means you have no say in the rules that decide control. Fifth, the reserve has no timeline: it does not say how many months it lasts or in what case.

Boardroom drill

Explain the capital stack to a board in two minutes. Try it now, aloud, then compare with this model answer.

Model answer: "Our project is funded by four layers, repaid in order. Senior debt covers the first 60 percent of cost, mezzanine the next 15, preferred equity the next 10, and our common equity the top 15. If value falls, losses start at the top, so our equity is the cushion. We tested coverage through every cash-pay layer, not just the senior loan: income can fall about 23 percent before the mezzanine is uncovered, and about 8 percent before the preferred return is, so we made the preferred return accrue in years one and two. The intercreditor terms are agreed and give a 30-day cure period and a qualified transferee test we can live with. Our downside, income down 10 percent and the cap rate up a point, keeps both lenders whole and costs our equity most of its value, which is the risk we are being paid to take."

What the board will ask next

Expect three follow-up questions after the two minutes, and have one-sentence answers ready. "What happens if the cap rate moves two points, not one?" Answer with the value and which layer it reaches. "Who are the mezzanine and preferred investors, and what do they want?" Answer with their track record and whether they lend to earn or to own. "What is our personal exposure?" Answer with every guarantee, its cap and its trigger. If you cannot answer any of the three in a sentence, that is the gap to close before the meeting, not during it.

Score yourself

Record your two-minute answer on your phone and score it 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: were the bands and coverage numbers right? Structure: did you open with the bottom line, then the layers, then the risk? Composure: was your pace steady and did you pause after the key number? The hard question: did you name the layer that fails first and what you did about it? A 3 on any line means you can explain it; a 5 means a lender would stop asking questions. Repeat the drill tomorrow and compare.

Where you will meet this again

The capital stack runs through the next several weeks. In week 38, the waterfall decides how the common equity's share is split between you and your investors, which only matters once the layers below have been paid. In weeks 39 and 40, the construction lender's conditions, covenants and guarantees are the senior layer's version of the triggers you negotiated on day six. In week 44, the stress tests you learn will be run against exactly the coverage figures you calculated on day five. Keep this week's seven-step test on one page and reuse it; you will need it every time a new layer is offered.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a stack that looks safe at the senior layer and fails at a junior one. The control is cumulative coverage and break-even for every layer on page one.

The beginner's mistake

Reading labels instead of remedies. Preferred equity can act like debt, and a mezzanine lender can move faster than a bank.

Callback

In week 13 we built sources and uses. The capital stack is the sources side read as a queue. Every time you write a sources and uses table now, add a column for each source's band, cost and remedy.

Recap

Position sets price, losses, and control. Test every layer, read every remedy, and size to in-place income.

speak: Mr Shabazz, week 37 in sixty seconds. The capital stack is a queue. Senior debt is repaid first, then mezzanine, then preferred equity, then common equity, and losses run the other way, from the top down. Position sets price: the higher the layer, the more it costs. Position also sets control, and the documents decide how fast: a mezzanine share pledge or a preferred investor's removal right can act faster than a mortgage. Stuyvesant Town showed what happens when the stack is sized to a business plan; Rule 37 says size to in-place income or a downside reserve. Junior capital magnifies outcomes and only helps when the asset outearns it. Read the intercreditor agreement for blockage, standstill, cure rights and the qualified transferee. Test cumulative coverage through every layer. And in the room, accept the rate and fight for the triggers.
terms: Capital stack — the full set of debt and equity funding a project, ordered by repayment and loss.
Intercreditor agreement — a contract between lenders to the same project setting out payment priority, enforcement rights and consents.
Cumulative coverage ratio — net operating income divided by the combined cash cost of a layer and every layer senior to it.

hostile.q: Your summary says leverage is 80 percent. Is that true?
hostile.a: Not if you count the preferred equity correctly. It is promised its return and capital ahead of the common, so it belongs in the stack: claims through preferred reach 90 percent of cost. I will restate the summary on that basis, show cumulative coverage through each layer, and confirm the intercreditor terms are agreed before closing.
